title: Returning References
intro: A function can return a reference only if it points into something that will still exist after the function returns. Usually that means into one of its inputs.

coming_from.go: Go lets you return `&s` for a local `s`: the compiler sees that `s` escapes the function and allocates it on the heap. (A Go function would normally just return the string.) Rust has no garbage collector, so you choose: return an owned `String`, or return a `&str` that points into one of the inputs.
coming_from.kotlin: Kotlin returns object references, and the garbage collector keeps whatever is still referenced alive. In Rust you choose: an owned `String` that the caller now owns, or a `&str` borrowed from an input, which works only while that input is still around.
coming_from.python: Python returns an object and keeps it alive for as long as anything refers to it. In Rust you return either an owned `String`, or a `&str` that borrows from an input and is valid only while that input lives.
coming_from.typescript: In TypeScript an object you return stays alive for as long as something refers to it. In Rust a returned `&str` must point into one of the inputs; anything made inside the function has to be returned as an owned `String`.
coming_from.java: Java returns object references, and the garbage collector keeps whatever is still referenced alive. In Rust a returned `&str` must point into one of the inputs; anything made inside the function has to be returned as an owned `String`: ownership moves to the caller, and the text is not copied.
coming_from.csharp: A returned `&str` is closest to a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` that points into the input. C# already refuses to return a span of a local or a `ref` to a local (CS8352, CS8168); Rust applies that rule to every reference, not only to ref structs. Anything the function makes itself is returned as an owned `String`.
coming_from.c: gcc warns when a function returns a pointer to a local array, but the program still builds, and using the pointer is undefined behaviour. In Rust it does not compile. Return an owned `String`, which frees itself, or a `&str` that points into an input.
coming_from.cpp: A returned `&str` is closest to a `std::string_view` into the input. Returning a reference to a local compiles in C++ (g++ warns) and is undefined behaviour when used; in Rust it is an error. Return a `String`, which is what returning a `std::string` by value is, and the usual fix in C++ too.

notes: Rule of thumb: if you made it inside the function, return it owned (`String`, `Vec`). If it is a piece of an input, you can return a reference (`&str`, `&[T]`).
`first_word` returns a `&str` that points into `g`. Rust remembers that link, so `w` can't outlive `g`.

This link is what Rust calls a lifetime. With one borrowed input, Rust fills it in by itself. With two, you must write it: `fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str`. The `'a` says "the result comes from one of these inputs, so use it only while both are alive".

faq.q: Do people really write lifetimes all over their code?
faq.a:
Not in every function. The compiler fills in the common cases (one reference in, a reference out; a method that returns a piece of `&self`), and a struct that owns its data (`String`, `Vec`, `Arc<T>`) needs no lifetime at all.

The two most common places for a lifetime you write by hand are a function that returns a reference and has more than one reference parameter, and a struct that holds a reference. The lifetimes lesson covers both, and more.

If your own code starts to feel like pointer gymnastics, returning an owned value is often a way out. Making an owned copy of borrowed data costs an allocation and a copy; that is usually fine until a measurement says otherwise.

gotcha.title: Returning a reference to something made inside the function
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Python, TypeScript and C#, returning something you made inside the function is normal: the garbage collector keeps it alive for as long as anything refers to it. In C and C++ the same shape is a bug that the compiler only warns about.
gotcha.rust_sees: `s` is owned by `make_greeting`, so it is freed at the closing `}`. A reference to it would point at memory that no longer holds the string.
gotcha.why: Rust has no garbage collector to keep `s` alive, and it does not move values to the heap on its own. `s` is freed at the closing `}`, so a reference to it would really dangle. That is the bug the C and C++ versions below get from this same code, and Rust turns it into a compile error. Nothing is wrong with the habit in a garbage-collected language; here you say who owns the result: return the `String` itself, which moves ownership to the caller without copying the text, or return a `&str` that points into an input.

go.says: Go runs this and prints hello rust. Go sees that `s` outlives the function and allocates it on the heap, so the pointer stays valid.

kotlin.says: Kotlin prints hello rust. Objects stay alive while something refers to them, so returning one made inside a function just works.

python.says: Python prints hello rust. The function returns the string object itself, and Python keeps it alive for as long as anything refers to it.

def make_greeting(name: str) -> str:
    s = f"hello {name}"
    return s
